modelAnswer: Danger triangle (upper lip/nose area) infection can spread to cavernous sinus via valveless facial vein and ophthalmic veins, causing cavernous sinus thrombosis with potentially fatal complications.

Scalp has rich blood supply from branches of external carotid and occipital arteries, causing profuse bleeding. The dense connective tissue between skin and aponeurosis prevents vasoconstriction, leading to continued bleeding.
Scalp wound complications include: profuse bleeding (rich vascularity), black eye (blood tracking through loose areolar tissue), nerve injury, and infection risk including cavernous sinus thrombosis.

explanation: Different cranial nerve nuclei supply specific structures. The facial nucleus supplies muscles of facial expression. Nucleus ambiguus supplies pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles. Dorsal motor nucleus of X supplies thoracic/abdominal viscera. Hypoglossal nucleus supplies tongue muscles.
keyConcept: Cranial nerve nuclei have specific structural targets

explanation: Cranial nerve nuclei are organized into columns: Somatic Efferent (eye/tongue muscles), Special Visceral Efferent (pharyngeal arch muscles), General Visceral Efferent (parasympathetic), and Visceral Afferent (taste/visceral sensation).
keyConcept: Cranial nerve nuclei organized into functional columns

explanation: Each nucleus column has distinct functions: SE controls voluntary eye/tongue movement; SVE controls mastication/facial expression/swallowing; GVE controls parasympathetic functions; Visceral afferent handles taste and visceral sensation.
keyConcept: Nucleus columns have distinct functional roles

explanation: Different nuclei serve specific functions: hypoglossal for tongue, nucleus ambiguus for swallowing/phonation, dorsal motor X for parasympathetic regulation, vestibular for balance, and cochlear for hearing.
keyConcept: Each cranial nerve nucleus serves specific function
